questions.q: What are the three categories this lesson teaches for sorting information in a dense scenario prompt?
options: Technical requirements, business requirements, and legal requirements
Explicit requirements, implied constraints, and decorative/scene-setting detail
High priority, medium priority, and low priority facts
Data requirements, integration requirements, and security requirements
questions.explain: These three categories — stated directly, following by necessary inference, or just context — are the sorting scheme this lesson teaches for a first read-through.

questions.q: Why are implied constraints the category candidates miss most often?
options: Because they are always stated in bold text, which candidates ignore
Because implied constraints never actually affect the final design
Because they require inference from a stated fact rather than being stated as a requirement themselves
Because scenarios never contain more than one implied constraint
questions.explain: Unlike explicit requirements, implied constraints follow necessarily from something stated but aren't flagged as requirements, which is exactly why they require careful inference to catch.

questions.q: What is the "removal test" this lesson teaches for telling an implied constraint apart from a decorative detail?
options: Asking whether the detail is mentioned more than once in the prompt
Asking whether a majority of classmates also noticed the detail
Asking whether the detail includes a specific number
Asking whether removing or changing the detail would change what a correct design would look like
questions.explain: If removing a detail wouldn't change any design decision, it was decorative; if removing it would allow a materially different (and simpler) design, it was doing real constraining work.

questions.q: Why does this lesson warn against treating every decorative detail as a hidden requirement, just to be safe?
options: Because over-indexing on irrelevant detail wastes scarce design and presentation time that should go toward the actual constraints that matter
Because decorative details are technically forbidden from appearing in any scenario
Because panels always penalize candidates who mention founding dates
Because decorative details are always factually incorrect
questions.explain: Spending limited design or presentation time 'solving' something nobody asked you to solve is its own failure mode, not a safer alternative to missing a real constraint.

questions.q: Why does this lesson's lab ask you to apply the technique to a brand-new scenario rather than re-analyzing a case study from Chapter 1?
options: Because Chapter 1's case studies no longer exist
Because new scenarios are always easier than the Chapter 1 case studies
Because re-analyzing scenarios whose constraints you already know doesn't build the skill of spotting them cold, which is what a timed board or live client meeting actually requires
Because the lab format requires exactly 400 words of scenario text
questions.explain: The skill only transfers if practiced on unfamiliar material — already knowing a scenario's constraints from earlier lessons removes the actual challenge of extracting them.
